sv_cgiab/cnv_with_bed_track.note: BAF added, and the coverage lane fixed so it can be read. Both halves of the note. (1) THE BAF TRACK: chr5 is the chromosome that most rewards one -- the benchmark calls three allelic states on it where chr3 (cnv_depth_baf) has two. Measured off the hosted bigWig per 2 Mb of het sites: chr5:20-22 Mb CN 2 (1|1) is 84% between 0.4 and 0.6, chr5:37-39 Mb CN 3 (2|1) is 45% at 0.15-0.4 and 49% at 0.6-0.85, chr5:60-62 Mb CN 1 (0|1) is 48% below 0.15 and 51% above 0.85 with nothing between. So the lane draws one band, then the 1/3-2/3 fork the tutorial's own table predicts for a gain, then the two LOH bands. (2) NORMALIZED READ DEPTH, and the tool that does it: that is what the coverage lane already was -- goleft indexcov normalizes each sample to its own median, which is the only reason the two rows can be read against each other. It did not LOOK like it because the display was on localsd autoscale while the walkthrough text tells the reader to apply a manual min/max cap: indexcov's centromere and repeat spikes run to 497, so every plateau sat in the bottom fifth of the lane as one cloud. Fixed 0..3 with crosshatches now, where the tumor's three levels (0.6 / 1.1 / 1.9 by median) step against the normal's flat 1.0. Caption and the walkthrough paragraph updated; viewport 690 -> 830.

sv_cgiab/driver_kras_gain.name: sv_cgiab/driver_kras_gain
sv_cgiab/driver_kras_gain.note: DONE, and with a published pipeline rather than a homegrown one. C-GIAB hosts the New York Genome Center's somatic pipeline run on this exact HG008-T/HG008-N pair, whose BIC-seq2 output is one log2 tumour-versus-normal copy ratio per segment: 196 segments genome-wide, so it loads as a 6 KB bedGraph. Both the normalization and the segmentation are theirs. Every figure gets it as its top lane, above the depth it summarizes, and the steps land where the benchmark says: chr3 p-to-q and chr18 over SMAD4 each move a full log2 unit (CN 1 to CN 2), and the KRAS tandem duplication sits log2(3/2) above its flanks with its edges on the called boundaries. Fixed range on all four so a step means the same thing from one figure to the next, which autoscale cannot do here because a homozygous deletion has no finite ratio and one such segment flattens a whole chromosome. Shown as published, not re-centred: BIC-seq2 normalizes on total read counts and HG008-T is hypodiploid, so the balanced baseline sits above zero. The recipe is in the tutorial and in scripts/build_sv_visualization_cgiab.sh (a 20 KB download and one awk).

sv_cgiab/cnv_depth_baf.name: sv_cgiab/cnv_depth_baf
sv_cgiab/cnv_depth_baf.note: DONE, and with a published pipeline rather than a homegrown one. C-GIAB hosts the New York Genome Center's somatic pipeline run on this exact HG008-T/HG008-N pair, whose BIC-seq2 output is one log2 tumour-versus-normal copy ratio per segment: 196 segments genome-wide, so it loads as a 6 KB bedGraph. Both the normalization and the segmentation are theirs. Every figure gets it as its top lane, above the depth it summarizes, and the steps land where the benchmark says: chr3 p-to-q and chr18 over SMAD4 each move a full log2 unit (CN 1 to CN 2), and the KRAS tandem duplication sits log2(3/2) above its flanks with its edges on the called boundaries. Fixed range on all four so a step means the same thing from one figure to the next, which autoscale cannot do here because a homozygous deletion has no finite ratio and one such segment flattens a whole chromosome. Shown as published, not re-centred: BIC-seq2 normalizes on total read counts and HG008-T is hypodiploid, so the balanced baseline sits above zero. The recipe is in the tutorial and in scripts/build_sv_visualization_cgiab.sh (a 20 KB download and one awk). FOLLOW-UP: the lane now covers the whole tutorial rather than the four figures this review round named. sv_cgiab/cnv_with_bed_track (whole chr5) leads with it over the indexcov scatter, and sv_cgiab/driver_cdkn2a_deletion gained what turned out to be its strongest evidence: BIC-seq2 segments the focal homozygous deletion at chr9:21,952,524-21,972,302, the benchmark SV_75 interval to within a few dozen bp, so the segment edges, the tumour coverage cliff, the read drop-out and the CN 0 call are four independent lanes on the same two breakpoints. The track is also in demos/cgiab/config.json now and deployed, so it is available to anyone opening the demo rather than only to figures that declare it as a session track.

pangenome/local_subgraph.name: pangenome/local_subgraph
pangenome/local_subgraph.note: Answered, and the answer is measured rather than argued: extracting more data does NOT recover it. In ecoli_pggb.segs.bed.gz the blunt node is segment 176693, 93 bp, rank 1, CFT073 only, and ecoli_pggb.links.bed.gz gives its two links as 176689 at K12:1,004,686 and 178029 at K12:997,574. So it is a 7.1 kb deletion, not an extraction artifact, and the window holding both anchors is 7.4 kb -- which odgi extract -E returns as 6,361 segments (K12:1,000,500-1,008,900) against the 48 here, because a base-level pggb graph averages ~17 bp per segment. odgi extract -c 1 fetches the far anchor alone and is worse: that node's own two ends are then open and it anchors 7 kb off the left of the linear view. What changed instead is that the figure now names the EVENT rather than the cut. If you want the fixed palette anyway, that is a core change to randomColor plus its test, not a spec edit; say the word. PALETTE NOW DONE, in randomColor itself rather than in this spec. The complaint was right and the diagnosis was that it reads as random RGB — which it literally was: the hash mapped straight into HSL, whose hue wheel spends a quarter of itself on greens that look identical and a sliver on yellow, and which at one nominal lightness gives glaring yellows beside murky blues. That unevenness is the whole difference between a hash palette and a curated one. Chromosome painting hashed a refName into nine category10 slots (the tenth, grey, is dropped because a grey ribbon reads as broken), so any genome with ten or more chromosomes re-used colors and rice's twelve were a guaranteed three-way collision. Fixed where it belongs: the display knows the anchor assembly's own refName order and passes it down, and each chromosome takes the next hue on the golden angle at the 70%/50% the reference-position ramps use. The golden angle rather than an even spread over the circle is not decoration, and the first render proved it: a refName list is not a chromosome list, rice's chrom.sizes has 30 entries for 12 chromosomes plus organelles and scaffolds, so i/N*360 squeezed every chromosome into the first 132 degrees and painted the whole figure red-through-green. A stride does not care how long the tail is and repeats only after 144 entries, which no karyotype reaches. Twelve distinct hues now, and the same fix lands on every colorBy query/target/reference figure -- hs1_vs_mm39 was 24 human chromosomes into 9 slots. SAME SCALE APPLIED, and of the three OrthoFinder figures this is the one I would revert. This set spans nearly eightfold (brachypodium 0.27 Gb to maize 2.14 Gb), so on one scale rice and brachypodium are stubs, maize is the only row with any width, and over half the frame is white. The chromosome names are gone from every row but maize. It is applied because you asked for it on both, and the caption now states the spread honestly, but say the word and it comes back off. The measurement behind the judgement: the three sets' size ratios are wheat 3.6x, vertebrates 3.4x, grasses 7.9x, and the shared scale is worth its whitespace at the first two. PALETTE IS BACK, and it is the palette rather than a ramp. Chromosome painting still assigns BY POSITION in the anchor assembly's own refName order -- that is what fixed the colour re-use -- but a position now indexes category10-minus-grey, the exact nine the previous build hashed into, instead of taking the next hue on the golden angle at HSL 70%/50%. Nine do not cover a karyotype, so each lap re-lights the same hues in OKLCH (core's new `relight`): deep first, then pale, because these ribbons draw at alpha 0.06 over white and a pale colour at 0.06 is one a reader cannot see. It is not the weaker option for telling chromosomes apart, which is what the ramp was reached for: closest pair in OKLab over 24 positions is 0.077 for the laps against 0.019 for the golden angle, since an even circle in HSL's hue is not perceptually even. Pinned by tests (the first nine ARE the palette; a lap re-lights rather than repeats). Regenerated across every chromosome-painting figure: the three orthofinder rows, grape_peach_cacao{,_gene_orthologs}, linear_synteny and hs1_vs_mm39_synteny. sameScale untouched this pass -- the standing offer to drop it from this one spec still stands.

tcga/mutations_tp53_subtype.note: FIXED, and it was a real bug rather than a drawing choice. The matrix lays out one column per feature in the order the worker returns them, and for a horizontally flipped view it mirrored that order to n-1-i. Both halves assumed the features arrive genomic-ascending, which nothing established: getFeaturesInMultipleRegions merges the per-region fetches and emits them as they land, so with one region it looked fine and TP53 with introns collapsed is where it broke -- six reversed regions, six interleaved fetches, a mirror applied to an order already roughly descending. The matrix has since been put on the same convention the LD display and hic already use -- the worker reflects each region's run onto itself (orderByScreenPosition) and no consumer carries an orientation, so `flipped`, `mirrorColumnIndex` and the shader uniform are gone and a view with mixed forward and reversed regions works too, which one global mirror could not express. CORRECTION to an earlier version of this note: I also had the ordering helper dedupe features, and said that dropped a duplicate column. It dropped nothing. This callset is SNVs and small indels -- over the six collapsed TP53 exons the longest REF allele is 30 bp against introns hundreds of bp wide, 210 records in and 210 columns out -- so nothing spans two fetched regions. The dedupe is removed and both TCGA figures re-render byte-identical without it.
